summary: The note covers how high-altitude space weather such as solar flares, geomagnetic storms and cosmic rays threatens avionics and passengers, prompted by an October 15, 2023 transatlantic navigation anomaly. It surveys responses including Faraday cages, resilient materials, AI/machine learning detection, revised FAA and ICAO guidelines, pilot training, and the ESA-led SWIFT program for international collaboration.
one_line: Space weather threatens aircraft avionics, and industry, AI, regulators and international programs like SWIFT are building defenses after an October 2023 incident.
key_facts: On October 15, 2023, a transatlantic flight experienced navigation system anomalies, likely caused by charged particles from a solar flare; the crew maintained control and passenger safety.
Airlines flying at higher altitudes for fuel efficiency and reduced air resistance face greater exposure to high-energy particles.
Cosmic radiation, mostly from solar events, can penetrate aircraft walls and disrupt electronics, potentially affecting flight controls, communications, and passenger and crew health.

Dr. Stephanie Green, a space weather physicist, said at the Aerospace Safety Symposium on November 7, 2023 that the industry 'has reached a turning point' and needs a proactive approach to avionics protection.
Faraday cages around sensitive electronics, enclosures of conductive material, are gaining favor to block external electric fields.
Angela Ramirez, a materials engineer, said at the Aviation Technology Conference on December 1, 2023 that materials must withstand mechanical stresses and high-energy particle bombardment.
Jason Lee, a tech entrepreneur, said at the AI for Aviation Safety workshop on January 20, 2024 that AI can foresee avionic disruptions before they happen; his company integrates AI into avionics.
AI in avionics software can detect the onset of space weather perturbations and trigger corrective actions in milliseconds, faster than human reflexes.
The FAA and ICAO are revising operational guidelines and mandating stricter reporting and monitoring protocols for space weather risks.
Pilot training now includes modules on electronics anomalies caused by space weather.
On February 4, 2024, the FAA's Office of Aerospace Medicine, led by Dr. Robert Castle, proposed new standards for space weather event forecasting and communication.
On March 10, 2024, the ESA announced SWIFT (Space Weather Initiative for Flight Technology), uniting aerospace companies, research institutions and airlines.
Paolo Nespoli, a former astronaut and SWIFT advisor, called the collaboration 'unprecedented but necessary'.
